Attention must be paid to the direction of the force relative to the displacement, because only the component of force along the displacement contributes to work. This node builds directly on the earlier idea that energy is the capacity to do work, and it prepares the ground for the study of power and the work-energy theorem in later classes.
eli5: Imagine you push a toy car. You only did "work" on it if it actually moved in the direction you pushed. Push a wall that won't budge? No work, even if you sweat. Carry your school bag while walking forward? The bag moves forward but your lifting force is upward, so that lift does no work on the bag. Work is measured in joules: one joule is the work of pushing with a 1 newton force through 1 metre -- like lifting a small apple up by one metre.

misconceptions.belief: If I am pushing something hard and I feel tired, I must be doing work.
misconceptions.correction: In physics, work is done only when the force causes displacement in its own direction. The 2024 CISCE examiner report observed that candidates were "not clear with the concept and answered by guesswork." Pushing a stationary wall produces no displacement, so W = 0 regardless of effort. Tiredness is a biological sensation, not a measure of mechanical work.

misconceptions.belief: Carrying a bag while walking means I am doing work on the bag.
misconceptions.correction: The upward (lifting) force you exert on the bag is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement. Since the component of force along the displacement is zero, the work done by the lifting force on the bag is zero. Work requires displacement in the direction of the force, not just any motion.

misconceptions.belief: Any displacement in the problem can be plugged into W = F x s.
misconceptions.correction: The 2024 examiner specifically noted that "for selecting the displacement, the direction of force was not taken into consideration... many candidates selected the height 3 m instead of length." You must use the displacement measured in the direction of the force whose work you are calculating, not just any distance mentioned in the question.

misconceptions.belief: It is fine to write just the final number.
misconceptions.correction: The 2020 and 2024 examiner reports both flag missing units and missing formulae. Always write W = F x s, substitute with units (e.g., 5 N x 2 m), and give the answer as "10 J". Omitting the unit joule loses marks even when the number is correct.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define work and state its SI unit. Express the unit in terms of newton and metre.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Work is said to be done when a force acts on a body and the body is displaced in the direction of the force. The two conditions are that a force must act and that displacement must occur along the direction of that force. The quantitative measure is given by W = F x s, where F is the force and s is the displacement in the direction of the force. The SI unit of work is the joule, symbol J. One joule is defined as the work done when a force of one newton displaces a body through one metre in the direction of the force, so 1 J = 1 N x 1 m = 1 Nxm. A convenient way to picture one joule is the work needed to lift a 1 N apple (about a 100 g apple) through a height of 1 m. Work is a scalar quantity, so it has only magnitude and no direction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A porter walks 20 m horizontally on a level platform carrying a 30 kg suitcase on his head. Explain why the work done by the upward force exerted by the porter on the suitcase is zero, even though the suitcase is clearly moving.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The porter exerts an upward force on the suitcase equal to its weight, which is about 30 kg x 10 N/kg = 300 N, directed vertically upwards. While he walks, the suitcase does move, but its displacement is horizontal, along the platform. Work is defined as W = F x s only when the displacement s is measured in the direction of the force F. Here the angle between the upward force and the horizontal displacement is 90 deg , so the component of the lifting force along the direction of motion is zero. Therefore the work done by the lifting force on the suitcase is zero. This does not mean the porter does no work at all -- he does work against friction between his feet and the ground to walk, and his muscles consume energy -- but the work done by the specific upward force on the suitcase is zero. This is a classic example of force perpendicular to displacement producing no mechanical work on the object.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes: "Since work = force x displacement, any time a body moves under a force, work is always equal to the force multiplied by the distance travelled." Evaluate this statement, pointing out what is correct, what is incomplete or misleading, and give a corrected version with a worked example.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is partly correct but misleadingly incomplete, and it captures exactly the kind of error CISCE examiners flagged in 2024 when candidates picked the wrong displacement. The correct part is that work does involve the product of a force and a displacement, and the unit does come out as the joule (Nxm). However, the statement is misleading in two important ways. First, it ignores direction: the displacement that appears in W = F x s must be the displacement in the direction of the force, not just any distance the body happens to travel. If the force is perpendicular to the motion, the work done by that force is zero, no matter how large the distance. If the force is at some angle, only the component of the force along the displacement contributes. Second, the phrase "any time a body moves under a force" is too broad: a body can move at constant velocity with no net external force acting (Newton's first law), in which case the net work done on it is zero even though it has travelled a distance. A corrected version would read: "The work done by a constant force on a body equals the magnitude of the force multiplied by the displacement of the body in the direction of the force; if the displacement is perpendicular to the force, the work done by that force is zero." Worked example: a force of 10 N acts horizontally on a box that moves 4 m horizontally. W = F x s = 10 N x 4 m = 40 J. But if the same 10 N force acted vertically upward while the box moved 4 m horizontally, the work done by that force would be 0 J, because the displacement in the direction of the vertical force is zero. The student's original statement would have given 40 J in both cases, which is wrong. Direction matters, and the examiner's 2024 comment that "the direction of force was not taken into consideration" shows this is a real and frequent error.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A boy pushes a cart with a steady horizontal force of 25 N. The cart moves 8 m along the floor in the direction of the push. Calculate the work done. Then state the work done by the same force if the cart had not moved at all.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: We use the formula W = F x s. Here the force F = 25 N acts horizontally and the displacement s = 8 m is in the same horizontal direction, so the conditions for work are satisfied. Substituting: W = 25 N x 8 m = 200 J. The work done by the boy on the cart is 200 joules. If the cart had not moved, the displacement s would be 0 m. Then W = 25 N x 0 m = 0 J. This illustrates the first condition for work: a force must act AND displacement must occur. No matter how large the force, with zero displacement the work done is zero -- like pushing a solid wall that does not budge. Note that the answer must carry the unit joule; writing only "200" without the unit would lose marks, as flagged in the CISCE examiner reports.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a short worksheet of two original numerical problems on work for a Class 8 peer, each illustrating a different one of the "no work done" cases, and provide the full solutions with formula, substitution, and unit.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Problem 1 (no displacement case): "A girl pushes a heavy wooden almirah with a force of 60 N for 10 seconds, but the almirah does not move. Calculate the work done by the girl on the almirah." Solution: Formula W = F x s. Force F = 60 N, displacement s = 0 m (the almirah does not move). Substituting: W = 60 N x 0 m = 0 J. So no work is done on the almirah, because although a force acts, there is no displacement. Problem 2 (force perpendicular to displacement case): "A student holds a 5 kg book bag in her hand and walks 12 m forward along a straight corridor at a steady height. Calculate the work done by the upward force she exerts on the bag." Solution: The upward force equals the weight of the bag, F = 5 kg x 10 N/kg = 50 N, directed vertically upward. The displacement s = 12 m is horizontal, perpendicular to the force. The displacement in the direction of the upward force is zero. So W = F x s_along_force = 50 N x 0 m = 0 J. The work done by the lifting force on the bag is zero, illustrating that a force perpendicular to the displacement does no work on the object. Both problems train the peer to check the two conditions for work before reaching for the formula.

masteryCriteria: Can state that work is done only when a force causes displacement in the direction of the force, and write the formula W = F x s; can state that the SI unit of work is the joule (J) with 1 J = 1 Nxm, and picture it as lifting a 1 N apple through 1 m; can calculate work done given force and displacement (e.g., 25 N x 8 m = 200 J) with correct formula, substitution, and unit; can identify the three cases where no work is done (no displacement, force perpendicular to displacement, no applied force) and justify W = 0 for each.

title: Kinetic energy (calculation)
subject: physics
definition:
Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy possessed by a body by virtue of its motion. Any body that is moving -- whether a rolling cricket ball, a flowing river, a gust of wind, or a speeding car on the Mumbai-Pune Expressway -- carries kinetic energy because work was done on it at some point to bring it from rest to its present speed. The quantitative definition follows directly from the work concept: the kinetic energy of a body equals the work required to accelerate it from rest to its current velocity. This gives the formula KE = 1/2mv^2, where m is the mass of the body in kilograms (kg) and v is its velocity in metres per second (m/s). The factor 1/2 arises because the average force during uniform acceleration from rest to v is half the final force value, and the square on velocity reflects that the work done grows with the square of the speed attained. The SI unit of kinetic energy is the joule (J), where 1 J = 1 kgxm^2/s^2; one joule is the kinetic energy of a body of mass 2 kg moving at 1 m/s (1/2 x 2 x 1^2 = 1 J). Kinetic energy is a scalar quantity -- it has magnitude but no direction -- and is a form of mechanical energy.

The dependence of KE on mass is linear: if the mass doubles while velocity stays the same, KE doubles. For example, a truck of mass 2000 kg moving at 10 m/s has KE = 1/2 x 2000 x 10^2 = 100,000 J, which is exactly twice the KE of a car of mass 1000 kg at the same speed (50,000 J). The dependence on velocity is quadratic (the v^2 relationship): if the velocity doubles while mass stays the same, KE becomes four times; if velocity triples, KE becomes nine times. A car moving at 60 km/h therefore has four times the kinetic energy of the same car at 30 km/h, which is why braking distance rises sharply with speed and why high-speed crashes are so destructive. Conversely, if velocity is halved, KE drops to one-fourth. This v^2 dependence is the single most important quantitative idea in this node and is frequently tested in ICSE numerical problems. Common examples used to illustrate KE include a moving car, flowing water (which is harnessed in hydroelectric plants such as the Bhakra Nangal dam), and wind (harnessed by wind farms in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat). Numerical problems require substituting mass and velocity into KE = 1/2mv^2, ensuring consistent SI units, and comparing KE values for bodies of different masses or speeds.
eli5: Imagine two balls rolling down a hill -- a tiny marble and a heavy football. The heavier one hits harder, and the faster one hits much harder still. Kinetic energy is a number that tells you exactly how hard. The rule is: take half the mass, multiply by speed times speed. So if you double the speed, the energy becomes four times bigger -- speed matters a lot more than weight!

misconceptions.belief: Doubling the velocity doubles the kinetic energy." This is the most common error and matches the CISCE examiner observation (2023, Q15) that "most of the candidates were not able to apply the correct formula of energy for the calculation.
misconceptions.correction: KE depends on v^2, not v. Doubling velocity multiplies KE by 2^2 = 4; tripling velocity multiplies KE by 3^2 = 9. Always square the velocity before multiplying by 1/2m.

misconceptions.belief: Forgetting to square the velocity and computing 1/2 x m x v instead of 1/2 x m x v^2. The CISCE PPA repeatedly flags "incorrect formula" application.
misconceptions.correction: write KE = 1/2mv^2 explicitly, square v first, then multiply. For v = 20 m/s, v^2 = 400, not 20.

misconceptions.belief: Using non-SI units (km/h for velocity, g for mass) and getting an answer that is not in joules. The 2024 examiner comment stresses: "Advise students to express every physical quantity with proper unit.
misconceptions.correction: always convert mass to kg and velocity to m/s before substituting. 36 km/h = 36 x (1000/3600) = 10 m/s.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define kinetic energy and state its SI unit and formula. Explain what each symbol in the formula represents.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body by virtue of its motion. It is the work required to accelerate a body from rest to its current speed. The formula is KE = 1/2mv^2, where m is the mass of the body in kilograms (kg) and v is its velocity in metres per second (m/s). The factor 1/2 arises from the average force during acceleration from rest, and the square on v reflects that the work done grows with the square of the speed. The SI unit of kinetic energy is the joule (J), where 1 J = 1 kgxm^2/s^2. Kinetic energy is a scalar quantity and a form of mechanical energy. For example, a body of mass 2 kg moving at 1 m/s has KE = 1/2 x 2 x 1^2 = 1 J. Common examples include a moving car, flowing water in a river, and wind turning a windmill. Any object that is moving -- from a rolling ball to a flying bullet -- possesses kinetic energy, and the greater its mass and the greater its velocity, the greater is its kinetic energy.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A car of mass 1000 kg is moving at 15 m/s. The driver accelerates to 30 m/s. By what factor does the kinetic energy increase? Explain the reasoning using the formula.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Initial KE = 1/2 x 1000 x (15)^2 = 1/2 x 1000 x 225 = 112,500 J. Final KE = 1/2 x 1000 x (30)^2 = 1/2 x 1000 x 900 = 450,000 J. The ratio of final to initial KE is 450,000 / 112,500 = 4. So the kinetic energy becomes four times its original value. The reasoning is that kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity (the v^2 relationship). When velocity doubles from 15 m/s to 30 m/s, the factor by which velocity changes is 2, and since KE proportional to v^2, the kinetic energy changes by 2^2 = 4. The mass stays the same, so only the velocity change matters. This is why a small increase in speed causes a large increase in kinetic energy, and it explains why braking distance and collision damage rise sharply with speed. If the velocity had tripled, KE would become nine times; if halved, KE would drop to one-fourth. This quadratic dependence is the most important quantitative relationship in this topic.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student claims that a heavy truck of mass 5000 kg moving at 10 m/s has more kinetic energy than a small car of mass 1000 kg moving at 25 m/s, because the truck is five times heavier. Evaluate this claim by calculating both kinetic energies and judging whether mass or velocity dominates.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The claim is incorrect, and the calculation shows why. For the truck: KE_truck = 1/2 x 5000 x (10)^2 = 1/2 x 5000 x 100 = 250,000 J. For the car: KE_car = 1/2 x 1000 x (25)^2 = 1/2 x 1000 x 625 = 312,500 J. Although the truck has five times the mass of the car, the car actually has more kinetic energy (312,500 J vs 250,000 J) because its velocity is 2.5 times greater, and kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity. The velocity factor contributes (2.5)^2 = 6.25, while the mass factor contributes only 5. Since 6.25 > 5, the car's higher speed more than compensates for its lower mass. This illustrates a key principle: because KE depends on v^2, velocity has a stronger influence on kinetic energy than mass does. A small, fast object can carry more kinetic energy than a large, slow one -- which is why a bullet, despite having a tiny mass, can be lethal due to its enormous velocity. The student's reasoning over-emphasises mass and ignores the quadratic effect of velocity. A balanced analysis must consider both factors, with special attention to the squared velocity term. In real-world contexts such as road safety, this is why reducing speed is far more effective at reducing collision energy than reducing vehicle mass.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Calculate the kinetic energy of a cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg bowled at 40 m/s. Then calculate the kinetic energy of a truck of mass 4000 kg moving at 10 m/s. Compare the two and comment.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For the cricket ball: KE = 1/2 x m x v^2 = 1/2 x 0.15 x (40)^2 = 1/2 x 0.15 x 1600 = 120 J. For the truck: KE = 1/2 x 4000 x (10)^2 = 1/2 x 4000 x 100 = 200,000 J. The truck has vastly more kinetic energy -- about 200,000/120 ~= 1667 times that of the cricket ball. This is because, although the ball is much faster (40 m/s vs 10 m/s), the truck's mass is about 26,667 times the mass of the ball (4000 kg vs 0.15 kg). The mass ratio dominates the velocity-squared ratio here: the ball's v^2 is 1600 while the truck's v^2 is only 100, a factor of 16 in favour of the ball, but the mass factor of ~26,667 overwhelms it. This shows that when mass differences are extreme, even a large velocity advantage cannot compensate. However, the ball's 120 J is still significant -- concentrated on a small area, it can do considerable damage to stumps or a batsman, illustrating that kinetic energy depends on both how the energy is delivered and the context.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple experiment using a marble rolling down a smooth inclined ramp to demonstrate that kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity. Describe what you would measure, what you would vary, and how you would conclude that KE proportional to v^2.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Set up a smooth inclined ramp of fixed length and let a marble roll down from different heights. At the bottom, place a small wooden block that the marble strikes; the distance the block slides along a rough horizontal surface is proportional to the work done on it, which equals the marble's kinetic energy at impact. Release the marble from height h, then from 2h, then from 3h. By energy conservation (which we will study later), the velocity at the bottom is v = sqrt(2gh), so doubling h increases v by a factor of sqrt2 and tripling h increases v by sqrt3. Measure the block's sliding distance each time. If KE proportional to v^2, then since v^2 = 2gh, KE should be directly proportional to h -- so releasing from 2h should give twice the sliding distance, and from 3h should give three times. Measure v at the bottom using a stopwatch over a known short distance, or use a photogate if available. Plot sliding distance (proxy for KE) against v^2 -- a straight line through the origin confirms KE proportional to v^2. Plotting against v alone gives a curve, not a line, showing that KE is not directly proportional to v. This experiment converts the abstract formula into a visible, measurable relationship and reinforces that the squared velocity term is what governs kinetic energy.

masteryCriteria: Can define kinetic energy as the energy of motion and state the formula KE = 1/2mv^2 with SI unit joule (J); can calculate KE given mass (kg) and velocity (m/s) by squaring velocity first, e.g. KE of a 2 kg body at 3 m/s = 1/2 x 2 x 9 = 9 J; can explain that KE doubles when mass doubles (velocity fixed) and becomes four times when velocity doubles (mass fixed) due to the v^2 relationship; can convert non-SI units (km/h to m/s, g to kg) before substituting into the formula.

title: Potential energy (calculation, gravitational PE)
subject: physics
definition:
Potential energy is the energy stored in a body by virtue of its position or configuration. It is the energy a body possesses because of where it is placed or how its parts are arranged, and it is not actively doing work at the instant but is capable of doing work when released. There are two important forms at this level: gravitational potential energy and elastic potential energy. Gravitational potential energy is the energy stored in a body because of its height above a chosen reference level (usually the ground). The formula used to calculate it is PE = mgh, where m is the mass of the body in kilograms, g is the acceleration due to gravity (taken as 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth, often rounded to 10 m/s^2 for ICSE numerical problems), and h is the height of the body above the reference level in metres. The product mgh gives the gravitational potential energy in joules (J), the SI unit of energy. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton displaces a body by one metre in the direction of the force.

Because PE = mgh, the stored energy depends directly on three quantities: mass, height, and the value of g. Doubling the mass doubles the PE (a 2 kg book on a 5 m shelf stores twice the PE of a 1 kg book on the same shelf). Doubling the height also doubles the PE (the same 1 kg book on a 10 m shelf stores twice the PE it stores on a 5 m shelf). On the Moon, where g is about 1.6 m/s^2, the same book at the same height stores roughly one-sixth of the PE it stores on Earth, because g is smaller. This is why an astronaut can lift a heavy rock easily on the Moon -- the rock stores far less gravitational PE there.

Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a body when it is stretched or compressed from its natural shape and released to return to that shape. A stretched rubber band, a compressed spring, a bent bow, and a stretched slingshot all store elastic potential energy. When released, this stored energy is converted into kinetic energy of the moving part. Together, kinetic energy (energy of motion) and potential energy (energy of position or configuration) make up the mechanical energy of a body. Numerical problems at ICSE level ask students to calculate gravitational PE given mass, height, and g, to compare PE at two different heights, and to identify the energy conversion in everyday situations such as water behind a dam (gravitational PE) or a stretched spring (elastic PE). The reference level for height must always be stated, because PE is meaningful only relative to a chosen zero level.
eli5: Imagine lifting a brick onto a shelf. The higher you lift it, the more "ready energy" it has stored -- if it falls, it can do more damage. That stored energy is potential energy. Scientists count it with PE = mgh: how heavy the brick is (m), how strong gravity pulls (g), and how high the shelf is (h). A heavier brick, a higher shelf, or stronger gravity all mean more stored energy. A stretched rubber band also stores energy, but from being stretched, not from height.

misconceptions.belief: Any object placed at a height converts gravitational potential energy into the final energy shown." CISCE examiners (2024, Question on doorbell energy conversion) observed that some candidates wrote "gravitational potential energy to sound energy" for a doorbell, thinking that because the bell is fixed at a height, the source must be gravitational PE.
misconceptions.correction: Height alone does not make the source gravitational. A doorbell runs on electrical energy, which is converted to sound. Use PE = mgh only when something actually falls or is lifted and gravity is the real source of the stored energy.

misconceptions.belief: PE = mgh, so I just write the number; units are not important." CISCE examiners (2020, Question 4) repeatedly observed that "units were not written in the final answer" and that "calculation errors were common.
misconceptions.correction: Always state the unit joule (J) in the final answer. Without the unit, the number is meaningless and marks are deducted. Write the formula, substitute with units (kg, m, m/s^2), and end with "... J".

misconceptions.belief: Doubling the height more than doubles the PE, because the object is higher up.
misconceptions.correction: PE is directly proportional to height, not to the square of height. Doubling h exactly doubles PE (e.g. 2 kg at 5 m -> 98 J; 2 kg at 10 m -> 196 J). Only kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity; potential energy depends linearly on height.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define potential energy and state the formula for gravitational potential energy with the meaning of each symbol and the SI unit.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Potential energy is the energy stored in a body by virtue of its position or configuration. It is not doing work at the instant but is capable of doing work when released. Gravitational potential energy is the energy stored in a body because of its height above a chosen reference level. The formula is PE = mgh, where m is the mass of the body in kilograms, g is the acceleration due to gravity in m/s^2 (about 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth), and h is the height above the reference level in metres. The SI unit of potential energy is the joule (J), the same unit used for kinetic energy and for work. One joule equals the work done when a force of one newton displaces a body by one metre. For example, a 1 kg object raised 1 m above the ground on Earth stores PE = 1 x 9.8 x 1 = 9.8 J. Potential energy is meaningful only relative to a chosen zero level, usually the ground, so the reference level should always be stated.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A 3 kg flower pot sits on a balcony 5 m above the ground. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, calculate its gravitational PE. Then explain what happens to this PE if the same pot is moved to a balcony 15 m above the ground, and if the pot is taken to the Moon (g ~= 1.6 m/s^2) at the original 5 m height.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: On the 5 m balcony, PE = mgh = 3 x 9.8 x 5 = 147 J. If the pot is moved to a 15 m balcony, the height triples while mass and g stay the same, so PE becomes 3 x 9.8 x 15 = 441 J -- exactly three times 147 J. This shows PE is directly proportional to height: tripling the height triples the stored energy. If the same pot is taken to the Moon at the original 5 m height, g drops from 9.8 m/s^2 to about 1.6 m/s^2, roughly one-sixth of Earth's gravity. The PE on the Moon becomes 3 x 1.6 x 5 = 24 J, about one-sixth of 147 J. So PE is also directly proportional to g. The reasoning shows that PE depends on three factors -- mass, height, and gravity -- and changes in any one of them change the stored energy in the same ratio. A heavier pot, a higher balcony, or stronger gravity all mean more stored gravitational potential energy.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A ceiling fan mounted at a height of 3 m on the ceiling has gravitational potential energy, so when the fan is switched on, the electrical energy is first converted into gravitational potential energy and then into the kinetic energy of the rotating blades." Evaluate this statement and correct it.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is incorrect and confuses two different ideas. It is true that the fan, having mass and being at a height of 3 m above the floor, does possess gravitational potential energy relative to the floor: PE = mgh, where m is the mass of the fan. However, this gravitational PE is not involved at all when the fan is switched on. The fan does not fall or change its height when it rotates; its blades spin about a fixed axis at the same level. The energy conversion that actually takes place is electrical energy -> kinetic energy of the rotating blades (and some heat and sound due to friction and air resistance). The gravitational PE of the fan is a separate, stored quantity that would only come into play if the fan fell off the ceiling. The student has made the common error of assuming that because an object is at a height, every energy change it undergoes must involve gravitational PE. CISCE examiners have observed exactly this kind of confusion -- candidates wrote "gravitational potential energy to sound energy" for a doorbell simply because the bell was fixed at a height. The correct reasoning is to ask: is the object actually changing height, or is gravity the source of the energy being converted? If not, gravitational PE is not part of the conversion, even though the object does possess some PE by virtue of its position. The corrected statement is: "The fan has gravitational PE because of its height, but when switched on, electrical energy is converted into the kinetic energy of the rotating blades; the gravitational PE remains unchanged and is not part of this conversion."

diagnosticQuestions.question: A water tank of mass 500 kg is filled and placed on a rooftop 12 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s^2, calculate the gravitational PE of the water in the tank relative to the ground. If 200 kg of this water is released and falls to the ground level, how much PE is lost, and what is the PE of the remaining water?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The total PE of the filled tank is PE = mgh = 500 x 10 x 12 = 60 000 J, or 60 kJ. When 200 kg of water is released and falls to ground level, that 200 kg loses all its height, so the PE lost is 200 x 10 x 12 = 24 000 J, or 24 kJ. The remaining water has a mass of 500 - 200 = 300 kg, still at the same height of 12 m, so its PE is 300 x 10 x 12 = 36 000 J, or 36 kJ. Notice that 60 000 J - 24 000 J = 36 000 J, which confirms that the PE of the remaining water equals the original PE minus the PE lost by the released water. This shows PE is additive with mass: each kilogram at the same height stores the same amount of PE (here, 1 x 10 x 12 = 120 J per kg), and the total is simply the mass times the PE per kilogram. In a real dam, this same principle determines how much energy can be released -- the height of the water column and the mass of water behind the dam together set the gravitational PE available to be converted into electrical energy via turbines.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom demonstration that shows both gravitational potential energy and elastic potential energy being converted into kinetic energy. Describe the setup, the two energy conversions, and how you would use a measuring tape and a balance to estimate the gravitational PE numerically.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Use two demonstrations side by side. For gravitational PE: take a small steel ball of measured mass (say 0.05 kg, found using a balance) and release it from a measured height (say 1.5 m, found using a measuring tape) onto a soft sand tray. Before release, the ball has gravitational PE = mgh = 0.05 x 9.8 x 1.5 = 0.735 J. On release, this PE converts into kinetic energy as the ball falls, and on hitting the sand it does work by making a dent -- showing the stored PE has been released. For elastic PE: stretch a rubber band by a fixed amount and release it to launch a small paper pellet. Before release, the stretched rubber band stores elastic potential energy because it is deformed from its natural length; on release, this elastic PE converts into the kinetic energy of the moving pellet. Comparing the two shows the shared idea: in both cases, energy is stored because of a condition (height in one, stretch in the other) and is released as motion when that condition is allowed to change. To estimate the gravitational PE numerically, measure the mass of the ball with the balance in kilograms and the height with the tape in metres, then substitute into PE = mgh with g = 9.8 m/s^2. Repeat the drop from 0.5 m, 1.0 m, and 1.5 m to show that the dent in the sand gets deeper as the height -- and hence the PE -- increases, giving a visible, measurable link between the formula PE = mgh and a real effect.

masteryCriteria: Can define potential energy as the energy stored in a body due to its position or configuration; Can calculate gravitational potential energy using PE = mgh with correct SI units (joule), e.g. a 2 kg object at 10 m has PE = 2 x 9.8 x 10 = 196 J; Can explain that doubling mass or height doubles PE and that PE on the Moon is about 1/6 of PE on Earth for the same mass and height; Can distinguish gravitational PE (energy of height) from elastic PE (energy of stretch/compression) and give one example of each.

title: Energy transformation in daily life
subject: physics
definition: Energy transformation is the process by which energy changes from one form to another while the total amount of energy in the universe remains constant -- a principle known as the law of conservation of energy, which states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted from one form to another. In daily life, every device we use performs an energy conversion: an electric bulb converts electrical energy into light energy and heat energy (most of the electrical energy actually becomes heat, with only a small fraction emerging as visible light); an electric fan converts electrical energy into mechanical energy (the rotational kinetic energy of the blades) and a little heat and sound; a loudspeaker converts electrical energy into sound energy through the vibration of its diaphragm; and a solar cell converts light energy (from the sun) into electrical energy. Tracing these conversions produces an energy chain -- a sequence showing how energy passes from one form to the next, for example in a hydroelectric power station the stored gravitational potential energy of water in a high reservoir converts to kinetic energy as it falls, then to mechanical energy of the turbine, and finally to electrical energy in the generator. In mechanical systems, the most important interconversion is between potential energy (PE) and kinetic energy (KE). In a simple pendulum, at the highest point of its swing the bob is momentarily at rest, so its KE is zero and its PE is maximum; at the lowest point (the mean position) the bob moves fastest, so its KE is maximum and its PE is minimum (taken as the reference level). As the pendulum swings, PE continuously converts into KE on the way down and KE converts back into PE on the way up, so the total mechanical energy (PE + KE) remains constant in an ideal (frictionless) pendulum. The same interconversion occurs in a freely falling object: at the top, PE is maximum and KE is zero; as it falls, PE decreases and KE increases; just before hitting the ground, PE is minimum (zero if ground is the reference) and KE is maximum. In real systems some mechanical energy is lost to heat and sound due to air resistance and friction, but the total energy -- including the heat and sound produced -- still remains conserved. The law of conservation of energy therefore applies to every transformation, whether in a bulb, a fan, a pendulum, or a falling stone.
eli5: Energy is like money that can change currency but never vanish. A bulb spends electrical "rupees" and gets light and heat "rupees" back -- same total. A pendulum is a savings account that swaps between two pockets: high up it keeps the money as "height money" (potential energy), and low down it keeps it as "speed money" (kinetic energy). The total never changes; it just moves between pockets.

misconceptions.belief: A doorbell converts gravitational potential energy to sound energy because the bell is fixed at a height." CISCE examiners in 2024 reported several candidates writing this.
misconceptions.correction: A doorbell is an electrical device -- when the button is pressed an electric circuit closes, an electromagnet attracts a striker, and the striker hits the gong. The correct conversion is electrical energy -> sound energy (with a little heat). The height of the bell is irrelevant; rote-associating "height" with "gravitational PE" without thinking about the device's working is the error.

misconceptions.belief: In a pendulum the bob stops eventually, so energy is destroyed.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is not destroyed -- it is gradually converted into heat and sound due to air resistance and friction at the support. The mechanical energy (PE + KE) decreases, but the total energy including the heat and sound produced remains exactly conserved. The law of conservation of energy is never violated.

misconceptions.belief: At the lowest point of a pendulum the energy is zero.
misconceptions.correction: At the lowest point the PE is taken as the reference (zero), but the KE is maximum. The total mechanical energy is NOT zero -- it equals the original PE at the highest point. Confusing "PE = 0" with "total energy = 0" loses marks in numerical questions.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the energy conversion that takes place in (a) an electric bulb, (b) an electric fan, (c) a loudspeaker, and (d) a solar cell. State the law of conservation of energy.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (a) In an electric bulb, electrical energy is converted into light energy and heat energy -- most of the electrical energy actually appears as heat, with only a small part as visible light. (b) In an electric fan, electrical energy is converted into mechanical energy (the kinetic energy of the rotating blades), along with a small amount of heat and sound energy. (c) In a loudspeaker, electrical energy is converted into sound energy through the vibration of the diaphragm or cone. (d) In a solar cell, light energy from the sun is converted into electrical energy. The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system remains constant. In every device above, the input energy exactly equals the sum of all the useful output energy and any wasted heat or sound -- nothing is lost, only transformed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A simple pendulum bob of mass 250 g is pulled aside until its centre is 8 cm above the lowest point of its swing and then released. Assuming no energy loss, calculate (i) the potential energy at the highest point, (ii) the kinetic energy at the lowest point, and (iii) the speed of the bob at the lowest point. Take g = 10 m/s^2.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First convert the given data into SI units: mass m = 250 g = 0.25 kg, height h = 8 cm = 0.08 m, g = 10 m/s^2. (i) Potential energy at the highest point is PE = mgh = 0.25 x 10 x 0.08 = 0.20 J. (ii) By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the total mechanical energy at the highest point equals the total mechanical energy at the lowest point. At the highest point the bob is momentarily at rest, so KE = 0 and total energy = PE = 0.20 J. At the lowest point the PE is taken as the reference (zero), so the entire 0.20 J appears as kinetic energy. Therefore KE at the lowest point = 0.20 J. (iii) Using KE = 1/2 mv^2, we have 0.20 = 1/2 x 0.25 x v^2, which gives 0.20 = 0.125 v^2, so v^2 = 1.6 and v = 1.26 m/s. The key steps examiners look for are: stating the principle of conservation of energy in words, converting units, and giving the final answer with correct units.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes: "In a real pendulum the bob eventually comes to rest, so the law of conservation of energy is violated in everyday situations." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument and a final judgement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is incorrect, but it raises a reasonable observation that deserves careful analysis. It is true that a real pendulum does come to rest after some time -- its amplitude gradually decreases and finally becomes zero. If we look only at the mechanical energy (PE + KE) of the bob, it does indeed decrease, which might superficially suggest that energy is being "lost" or "destroyed". However, this is only an apparent loss. As the pendulum swings, two dissipative forces act continuously: air resistance on the bob and friction at the point of suspension. Both of these forces convert some of the pendulum's mechanical energy into other forms -- specifically heat energy (due to friction) and a small amount of sound energy. The faster the bob moves, the greater the air resistance, so more mechanical energy is converted to heat per swing, and the amplitude shrinks a little more each time. Eventually all of the original mechanical energy has been transformed into heat and sound, which are dissipated into the surrounding air and the support. If we could measure the heat gained by the air and the support, plus the sound energy radiated, and add it to the remaining mechanical energy of the bob, the total would exactly equal the initial potential energy given to the pendulum when it was first pulled aside. Therefore the law of conservation of energy is NOT violated -- it holds perfectly. What changes is only the form and location of the energy: mechanical energy of the bob becomes thermal energy of the surroundings. The student has confused a decrease in one particular form of energy (mechanical) with a decrease in total energy. The correct judgement is that the statement is false; the law of conservation of energy remains valid in the real pendulum, provided all forms of energy -- including heat and sound losses -- are accounted for.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Trace the complete energy conversion chain in a hydroelectric power station from water stored in a high reservoir to an electric bulb glowing in a distant home. Identify each form of energy in order.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A hydroelectric power station is a classic example of an energy chain with several linked conversions. (1) Water stored in a high reservoir behind the dam possesses gravitational potential energy because of its height above the turbines. (2) When the sluice gates open, water rushes down the penstock; the gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy of the flowing water. (3) The fast-moving water strikes the blades of a turbine, transferring its kinetic energy to the turbine wheel, which rotates -- the energy is now mechanical energy (rotational kinetic energy) of the turbine. (4) The turbine is coupled to a generator; the generator converts the mechanical energy into electrical energy through electromagnetic induction. (5) The electrical energy is transmitted through transmission lines to homes. (6) At the home, when this electrical energy reaches an electric bulb, the bulb converts it into light energy and heat energy. So the full chain is: gravitational PE -> kinetic energy of water -> mechanical energy of turbine -> electrical energy -> light energy + heat energy. At every stage the total energy is conserved; small amounts are lost as heat due to friction in the penstock, resistance in the wires, and so on, but those losses are also energy in another form.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom experiment using a small pendulum (a stone tied to a string) and a metre scale to demonstrate the interconversion of PE and KE. Describe what you would measure, what you would calculate, and how you would use the results to verify the law of conservation of mechanical energy.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Suspend a small stone of known mass (say 100 g = 0.1 kg) from a fixed support using a light string about 1 m long to form a simple pendulum. Mark the lowest point of the bob's swing on a vertical scale placed behind it; this is the reference level where PE = 0. Pull the bob sideways to a measured height h (say 10 cm = 0.1 m) above the reference and hold it -- at this instant the bob is at rest, so KE = 0 and PE = mgh = 0.1 x 10 x 0.1 = 0.1 J. Release the bob and observe it swing through the lowest point. To verify conservation, calculate the expected speed at the lowest point using 1/2 mv^2 = mgh, giving v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.1) = 1.41 m/s, and the expected KE = 0.1 J, which should equal the initial PE. In practice, measure the maximum speed at the lowest point (using a photogate if available, or by timing several swings and estimating) and compute the actual KE; it will be slightly less than 0.1 J because some energy is converted to heat and sound due to air resistance. The "missing" mechanical energy, when added to the measured KE, should account for the original 0.1 J, demonstrating that energy is conserved overall. The experiment shows PE -> KE on the downward swing and KE -> PE on the upward swing, with the sum PE + KE approximately constant, confirming the law of conservation of mechanical energy and illustrating how real losses appear as heat and sound.

masteryCriteria: Can state the energy conversion in each common device -- electric bulb (electrical -> light + heat), electric fan (electrical -> mechanical), loudspeaker (electrical -> sound), solar cell (light -> electrical), doorbell (electrical -> sound); can state the law of conservation of energy and explain that "lost" mechanical energy becomes heat and sound; can trace the PE--KE interconversion in a simple pendulum (PE max at extreme, KE max at mean, total PE + KE constant) and in a freely falling body; can solve a numerical using PE = mgh and KE = 1/2 mv^2 with correct SI unit conversions (g -> kg, cm -> m) and state the conservation principle in words.

title: Difference between energy and power
subject: physics
definition:
Energy is the capacity to do work, while power is the rate at which that work is done or that energy is used. This single distinction -- "how much" versus "how fast" -- is the heart of this node. In Class 6 (node c6_phy_017) you learned that energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules (J). In Class 8 (node c8_phy_016) you studied energy transformation, how energy changes from one form to another (chemical to electrical to light, for example) while the total is conserved. Now we add a new, complementary idea: power, which tells us how quickly that energy is being used or work is being done.

Power is defined by the formula P = W/t, where P is power, W is the work done (in joules), and t is the time taken (in seconds). The SI unit of power is the watt (W), named after James Watt, the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine. One watt is defined as one joule per second: 1 W = 1 J/s. This means a device with a power of 1 W uses 1 joule of energy every second. Larger units used in everyday life include the kilowatt (1 kW = 1000 W) and the megawatt (1 MW = 10^6 W). Another traditional unit still encountered in engines and pumps is the horsepower (1 hp ~= 746 W), which students should recognise but need not convert frequently at this level.

The crucial distinction is this: energy is a quantity (measured in joules), while power is a rate (measured in watts, which is joules per second). Two devices can deliver the same total energy but have very different power ratings. A 100 W bulb and a 40 W bulb both convert electrical energy into light and heat, but the 100 W bulb uses energy faster -- it consumes 100 joules every second compared with the 40 W bulb's 40 joules every second. If both are switched on for one hour, the 100 W bulb uses 100 x 3600 = 360 000 J, while the 40 W bulb uses only 40 x 3600 = 144 000 J. Same time, different energy consumed -- because their power differs.

Conversely, the same total energy can be delivered at different rates. A runner and a walker covering the same distance up a hill do the same work against gravity (same energy output), but the runner delivers that energy in a shorter time and therefore has a higher power. This is why power is best understood as the "speed of spending energy": energy is how much money you have, power is how fast you spend it.

Numerical problems at this level require calculating power from given work and time using P = W/t, and distinguishing energy from power in practical situations such as bulbs, fans, pumps, and lifts. Students must also recognise that the commercial unit of electrical energy, the kilowatt-hour (1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J), is a unit of energy (power x time), not of power -- a point CISCE examiners have repeatedly flagged in pupil performance analysis.
eli5: Think of energy as the money in your piggy bank and power as how fast you spend it. A 100 W bulb is a big spender -- it uses 100 joules every second. A 40 W bulb is a slow spender -- only 40 joules each second. Both use the same kind of energy, but one burns through it faster. So energy is "how much" (in joules) and power is "how fast" (in watts, which means joules per second).

misconceptions.belief: Power and energy are the same thing, just different units.
misconceptions.correction: They are different physical quantities. Energy is the capacity to do work, a quantity measured in joules. Power is the rate at which that work is done, measured in watts (joules per second). A 100 W bulb and a 40 W bulb differ in power even though both use electrical energy; over the same time the 100 W bulb consumes more energy. CISCE examiners (Question 1, 2020) flagged confusion between the unit of energy (kWh) and the unit of power (W) -- students must keep them separate.

misconceptions.belief: The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of power because it contains the word watt.
misconceptions.correction: The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy. It is power (kilowatt) multiplied by time (hour): 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J. The 2020 board answer key explicitly required "one kilowatt hour is the energy spent or work done by a source of power 1 kW in one hour" and the conversion 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J. Any unit of the form (power x time) is an energy unit.

misconceptions.belief: A more powerful device always uses more energy.
misconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. Power is the rate of use. A 1000 W heater run for 1 s uses 1000 J, while a 10 W LED run for 1 hour uses 10 x 3600 = 36 000 J. The lower-power device used more energy because it ran much longer. Energy = Power x Time, so both factors matter.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define power, state its SI unit, and write the formula relating power, work, and time.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Power is defined as the rate of doing work or the rate at which energy is used. Its SI unit is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s (one joule per second). The formula is P = W/t, where P is power in watts, W is the work done in joules, and t is the time taken in seconds. Larger units include the kilowatt (1 kW = 1000 W) and the megawatt (1 MW = 10^6 W). A traditional unit still seen on engine nameplates is the horsepower (1 hp ~= 746 W). The key idea is that power tells us how quickly work is being done, not how much work is done. For example, a 60 W bulb uses 60 joules of electrical energy every second it is switched on.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A 100 W bulb and a 40 W bulb are both switched on for 2 minutes. Explain which bulb uses more energy and why, and calculate the energy used by each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The 100 W bulb uses more energy because it has a higher power rating, meaning it converts electrical energy into light and heat at a faster rate. Power is the rate of energy use, so for the same time interval a higher-power device consumes more energy. Time = 2 minutes = 120 s. Energy used by the 100 W bulb = power x time = 100 W x 120 s = 12 000 J. Energy used by the 40 W bulb = 40 W x 120 s = 4800 J. The 100 W bulb uses 12 000 - 4800 = 7200 J more energy than the 40 W bulb in the same period. This illustrates the distinction: both bulbs use electrical energy, but the 100 W bulb uses it faster because power is the rate of energy consumption, not the amount of energy itself.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A 10 W LED lamp running for 10 hours uses more energy than a 2000 W electric kettle running for 1 minute, so the LED is more powerful than the kettle." Evaluate this statement, correcting any errors of reasoning.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement mixes up two different quantities -- energy and power -- and draws a wrong conclusion by confusing them. Let us separate the two. First, compute the energy used by each device. For the LED: energy = power x time = 10 W x (10 x 3600 s) = 10 x 36 000 = 360 000 J. For the kettle: energy = 2000 W x 60 s = 120 000 J. So the student is correct that the LED uses more total energy (360 000 J versus 120 000 J) -- but only because it runs for a much longer time (36 000 s versus 60 s), not because it is more powerful. The second half of the student's claim, "so the LED is more powerful than the kettle," is wrong. Power is the rate of energy use, and the kettle's power (2000 W) is two hundred times the LED's power (10 W). The kettle delivers energy far faster; it simply was switched on for a very short time. The student has conflated energy (the total, which depends on both power and time) with power (the rate, which is a property of the device alone). The correct conclusion is: the LED used more energy in this scenario because of its long running time, but the kettle is far more powerful because it uses energy at a much higher rate. This example captures the entire point of the node: energy answers "how much" and depends on power x time, while power answers "how fast" and is an intrinsic rate. A board examiner would expect the student to keep these two ideas cleanly separated and to support each conclusion with the calculation, exactly as done above.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A water pump lifts 150 kg of water through a vertical height of 8 m in 30 s. Take g = 10 m/s^2. Calculate the power of the pump in watts and in kilowatts.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First calculate the work done against gravity. Work W = mgh = 150 kg x 10 m/s^2 x 8 m = 12 000 J. This is the gravitational potential energy given to the water. Now apply the power formula P = W/t. Time t = 30 s. So P = 12 000 J / 30 s = 400 W. To express this in kilowatts, divide by 1000: 400 W = 0.4 kW. So the pump has a power of 400 W, or 0.4 kW. The steps illustrate the standard board-exam method: compute the work (or energy) first using the appropriate formula from earlier nodes, then divide by the time to obtain the power, and finally state the answer with the correct SI unit. Always include the unit; an answer of "400" without "W" would lose a mark.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple experiment using two bulbs of different power ratings (say 100 W and 40 W) and an electricity meter (in kWh) to demonstrate the difference between energy and power. Describe what you would measure, what you would expect to observe, and how the results illustrate the distinction.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Use a 100 W incandescent bulb and a 40 W bulb, a stopwatch, and a domestic electricity meter that reads in kilowatt-hours. Switch off all other appliances so only the test bulb draws power. First, switch on the 100 W bulb and record the meter reading; let it run for exactly 30 minutes (1800 s) and record the new reading. The difference gives the energy used in kWh. Repeat the same procedure with the 40 W bulb for the same 30 minutes. Expected observations: the 100 W bulb should cause the meter to advance by 100 W x 0.5 h = 0.05 kWh, while the 40 W bulb should advance by 40 W x 0.5 h = 0.02 kWh. The 100 W bulb makes the meter turn faster and advance more, showing it uses energy at a higher rate. The experiment illustrates the distinction as follows: the power rating (100 W or 40 W) is a fixed property of each bulb and tells us the rate of energy use -- that is power. The meter reading (in kWh) tells us the total energy actually consumed over the time interval -- that is energy. Same time, different energy consumed, because the powers differ. This cleanly separates "how fast" (power, in watts) from "how much" (energy, in kilowatt-hours), which is the central idea of this node.

masteryCriteria: Can define power as the rate of doing work using P = W/t and state the SI unit as the watt (1 W = 1 J/s); can distinguish energy (capacity to do work, measured in joules) from power (rate of using energy, measured in watts) in a clear two-part sentence; can calculate power from given work and time (e.g. 20 000 J in 40 s = 500 W) and energy from power x time (e.g. 100 W bulb for 120 s = 12 000 J); can recognise the kilowatt-hour (1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J) as a unit of energy, not power.
